UPSTREAM: kconfig: fix menuconfig on debian lenny In 60f33b8 (kconfig: get rid of stray a.o, support ncursesw, 2006-01-15), support to link menuconfig with ncursesw library was added. To compute the linker command option -l, we check "libncursesw.{so,a,dylib}" to allow ncursesw to be used as a replacement ncurses. However, when checking what header file to include, we do not check /usr/include/ncursesw directory. Add /usr/include/ncursesw to the list of directories that are checked. With this patch, on my Debian Lenny box with libncursesw5-dev package but not libncurses5-dev package, I can say "make menuconfig". BACKPORT: kbuild: Fix gcc -x syntax The correct syntax for gcc -x is "gcc -x assembler", not "gcc -xassembler". Even though the latter happens to work, the former is what is documented in the manual page and thus what gcc wrappers such as icecream do expect. This isn't a cosmetic change. The missing space prevents icecream from recognizing compilation tasks it can't handle, leading to silent kernel miscompilations. Besides me, credits go to Michael Matz and Dirk Mueller for investigating the miscompilation issue and tracking it down to this incorrect -x parameter syntax. BUG=None TEST=`make menuconfig` works again BRANCH=None Change-Id: I0e124932ae1cfc673921c2e4e0fdfdbe5f81478c Signed-off-by: Jean Delvare <jdelvare@suse.de> Acked-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org Cc: Bernhard Walle <bernhard@bwalle.de> Cc: Michal Marek <mmarek@suse.cz> Cc: Ralf Baechle <ralf@linux-mips.org> Signed-off-by: Michal Marek <mmarek@suse.cz> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/685958 Commit-Ready: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org> Tested-by: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Shawn N <shawnn@chromium.org>

UPSTREAM: menuconfig: fix extended colors ncurses support The ncurses library allows for extended colors. The support for extended colors support depends on wide-character support. ncurses headers enable extended colors (NCURSES_EXT_COLORS) only when wide-character support is enabled (NCURSES_WIDECHAR). The "make menuconfig" uses wide-character ncursesw library, which can be compiled with wide-character support, but does not define NCURSES_WIDECHAR and it's using headers without wide-character (and extended colors) support. This fixes problems with colors on systems with enabled extended colors (like PLD Linux). Without this patch "make menuconfig" is hard to use. BUG=None TEST=`make menuconfig` works again BRANCH=None Change-Id: I18443f720ebadb0ac535c66f3f06ecc91a22e800 Signed-off-by: Krzysztof Mazur <krzysiek@podlesie.net> Signed-off-by: Michal Marek <mmarek@suse.cz> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/685959 Commit-Ready: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org> Tested-by: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Shawn N <shawnn@chromium.org>

UPSTREAM: kconfig/lxdialog: rationalise the include paths where to find {.n}curses{,w}.h The current code does this: if [ -f /usr/include/ncursesw/curses.h ]; then echo '-I/usr/include/ncursesw -DCURSES_LOC="<ncursesw/curses.h>"' elif [ -f /usr/include/ncurses/ncurses.h ]; then echo '-I/usr/include/ncurses -DCURSES_LOC="<ncurses.h>"' elif [ -f /usr/include/ncurses/curses.h ]; then echo '-I/usr/include/ncurses -DCURSES_LOC="<ncurses/curses.h>"' [...] This is merely inconsistent: - adding the full path to the directory in the -I directive, - especially since that path is already a sub-path of the system include path, - and then repeating the sub-path in the #include directive. Rationalise each include directive: - only use the filename in the #include directive, - keep the -I directives: they are always searched for before the system include path; this ensures the correct header is used. Using the -I directives and the filename-only in #include is more in line with how pkg-config behaves, eg.: $ pkg-config --cflags ncursesw -I/usr/include/ncursesw This paves the way for using pkg-config for CFLAGS, too, now we use it to find the libraries. BUG=None TEST=`make menuconfig` works again BRANCH=None Change-Id: Ie0787f859e3a597d7e004bce0b4d2207009ed7c1 Signed-off-by: "Yann E. MORIN" <yann.morin.1998@free.fr> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/685961 Commit-Ready: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org> Tested-by: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Shawn N <shawnn@chromium.org>

CHROMIUM: Bluetooth: set Filter_Duplicates parameter to 0x00 for LE scanning This is eve only by using CONFIG_BT_EVE_HACKS flag. This sets the Filter_Duplicates parameter of LE Set Scan Enable command to LE_SCAN_FILTER_DUP_DISABLE (0x00). There is a conflict intention of receiving advertising reports in BlueZ where the Filter_Duplicates flag is set so the strict filtering with RSSI will be applied to Intel BT controllers. However BlueZ checks if HCI_QUIRK_STRICT_DUPLICATE_FILTER is set and restarts LE scan if the bit is set in order to obtain the advertising reports dropped due to the strict filtering. By setting the Filter_Duplicates, BlueZ can potentially receive more advertising reports. CHROMIUM: Bluetooth: btusb: remove HCI_QUIRK_STRICT_DUPLICATE_FILTER bit This is eve only by using CONFIG_BT_EVE_HACKS flag. This removes the HCI_QUIRK_STRICT_DUPLICATE_FILTER bit from the Intel USB driver block in btusb_probe(). There is a conflict intention on receiving advertising reports in BlueZ where the Filter_Duplicates flag is set so strict filtering with RSSI will be applied to Intel BT controllers. However, BlueZ checks if HCI_QUIRK_STRICT_DUPLICATE_FILTER is set and restarts LE scan if the bit is set in order to obtain the advertising reports dropped due to the strict filtering. By removing the bit, BlueZ will not frequently restart LE scanning. bluetooth: "Fix" sync of commands for adv & scan This is a very ugly hack, presented here in a very ugly way. The ugly way is basically how we deliver this only for eve and not affect other devices. The ugly hack is basically how we work aroung bluez's complete lack of synchronization. Let me explain. No, there is not time. Let me summarize: bluez has a boolean value for "are we scanning" which it updates inside the command-complete event handler. It also checks this in many places as a way to tell if the chip is or is not scanning. The issue is that some chips (like BCM's) let you disable something already disabled and do not raise a fuss. Other chips (like Intel's 7265) do raise a fuss if you try to disable scanning if it is already off. So why the issue? If the chip raises an error, bluez loses its marbles and gets out of sync with the chip. Basically it thinks the chip *IS* scanning while chip is not. There is no way out of this since any attempt to tell bluez to start scanning causes it to just reply with "already am" and any attempt to stop scanning sends the "scan disable" command to the chip and produces the same kind of error that got us into this mess. So how do we fix this? There isn't really a simple or elegant way. But the basic issue is that while a command to enable or disable scanning is in flight, any code in the stack will think scanning is still in the old state, while it may already be in the new state. This might cause more commands to be enqueued based on this errorneous information. To solve this we'd like to always have correct information. Sadly this is not easy. There is also a command queue, which at any point in time may have many command enqueued that affect scanning state. There are multiple ways to insert commands into it, and we do not want to instrument them all. So what do we do? First we add a second boolean bit for "scan state change command in flight". We set this when we *SEND TO THE CHIP* a command that affects scan state and clear it when a reply arrives. We also change all places that check the "are we scanning" state to properly consider this new variable as well. This will not solve the issue of many commands queued already. So it is still possible that while a "disable" was queued, another "disable" may be queued. To work around this we also track the current state in the lowest layer that actually sends commands to the chip and simply drop ones that would transition us to the same state that we're already in. The situation is actually weirder because there is a "restart" func in bluez all of whose callers seem to assume that it atomically toggles scanning off and back on if it is already on. No such atomicity exists in reality. Our hack covers up for this in most cases. Oh, and this same exact logic applies to "are we advertising" boolean and we treat it the same way. This really solves nothing, but it works around the issue well enough for our purposes. A proper fix would be a separate queue for state changes for "adv" and "scan" with proper suport for atomic "restart" requests. This queue would then submit actual commands to the chip's queue. since nobody else would do that, it would have no races. We have no time to produce such fixes, so for now you get to enjoy this dirty hack. This hack is based on initial work by josephsih@ who first figured out the proper place to filter all the low level commands as they are sent to the chip and the proper way to drop them. minigbm: add drv_bo_flush As an optimization, we would like to separate buffer flush/writeback and unmap. This patch adds the appropriate entry point in our internal driver API. Overall, the proposed flow is: - drv_bo_map(..) creates a mapping and associated metadata - drv_bo_flush(..) writes memory from any cache or temporary buffer back to memory - drv_bo_unmap(..) flushes, and frees the mapping and associated metadata. The drv_bo_flush function just does some sanity checks on the map data at this point, but otherwise is a no-op.
